clue.text: Disgruntled choirmaster, I'm leaving for another musical group

indicators.note: disgruntled suggests the choirmaster's letters are put out of sorts and rearranged
leaving tells us the letters of I'm go out of the choirmaster's pool before rearranging

explanation.surface: A fed-up choirmaster quits to join a different kind of ensemble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disgruntled' and 'leaving' work together: take I and M out of CHOIRMASTER to leave CHORASTER, then rearrange. 'Another' is fair because a choir is itself a musical group.
explanation.definitionFit: An orchestra is a large ensemble of instrumental players, a different kind of performing body from a choir.

clue.text: What's targeted on table dance after protest

indicators.note: after puts the dance later in the answer than the protest

parts.note: to object is to protest
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: Something aimed at during a party follows a demonstration.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition refers to snooker or pool: the object ball is the one the cue ball is played at.
explanation.definitionFit: In cue sports, the object ball is the ball the player aims to strike with the cue ball.

clue.text: What starts this clue is excellent

definitions.meaning: the first letter of the clue, printed in upper case
a dated British exclamation of approval, like splendid

explanation.walkthrough: The clue points at itself: its first letter is in upper case. 'Capital!' is a dated British expression of delight.
explanation.definitionFit: The opening W is printed as an upper-case letter, and capital is an old-fashioned British word for first-rate.

clue.text: Partly clear the ground

indicators.note: Partly says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Part of the land is being cleared.
explanation.definitionFit: Earth is soil, the ground underfoot.

clue.text: Trial marriages — they can last for days

parts.note: a test is a trial
matches are marriages, unions arranged between partners

explanation.surface: Trying out marriage first can lead to unions that go on for days.
explanation.walkthrough: Test matches are international cricket games lasting up to five days, which makes the definition fair.
explanation.definitionFit: International cricket fixtures of this kind are played over as many as five days.

clue.text: Cause of inflation in Mumbai? Right

indicators.note: in says the letters sit within the words that follow, across the end of Mumbai and start of Right

explanation.surface: Is rising prices in an Indian city the right worry?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inflation' suggests prices, but it is the blowing up of a tyre or balloon.
explanation.definitionFit: Pumping gas into a tyre or balloon is what inflates it.

clue.text: Work during strike and leave

indicators.note: during places one thing in the middle of another, so the work sits inside the strike

parts.note: to strike is to hit
OP is short for opus, a musical work

explanation.surface: Someone downs tools mid-strike and walks off the job.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests industrial action, but 'strike' is just HIT. HOP IT is British slang for 'go away'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hop it is an informal British command meaning go away, so it is a synonym for depart.

clue.text: Hard blows for some in agriculture

definitions.meaning: farm workers who cut and turn grass for fodder

explanation.definitionFit: A haymaker is a wild swinging punch, and also a farm worker who cuts and dries grass for fodder.

clue.text: Unfinished company scrutiny getting acclaim

indicators.note: unfinished means the company's abbreviation loses its last letter

parts.note: PLC is a public limited company in Britain
an audit is an official scrutiny of accounts

explanation.surface: A firm's half-done examination of its books still wins praise.
explanation.walkthrough: PLC (public limited company, a British firm listed on the market) cut short is PL; 'getting' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A plaudit is an expression of praise or applause.

clue.text: Nonsense, chum!

definitions.meaning: a friendly or brusque British form of address, like mate

explanation.walkthrough: 'Oi, tosh!' is a British way of addressing a man, often brusquely.
explanation.definitionFit: Tosh means rubbish talk, and in British slang it is also a casual form of address to a man, like mate.

clue.text: Punch book missing, taken by a joker

indicators.note: missing says the book is absent from the punch, so its letter drops out

parts.note: a jab is a quick punch
per means by, as in per post

explanation.surface: A comic magazine has lost an issue, and a prankster pockets it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Punch' looks like the British humour magazine, but it is a blow, JAB; with B gone it is JA, and 'taken by' attaches PER. 'Taken' and 'a' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: A japer is someone who plays jests or pranks, a prankster.

clue.text: Fine stuff comes out of these

definitions.text: Fine stuff comes out of these

parts.words: Fine stuff comes out of these
parts.note: read as praise for quality goods, but 'fine' means finely divided, a mist of droplets released from aerosol containers

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine stuff' suggests something of high quality; here it is a fine mist, as from paint or deodorant aerosols.
explanation.definitionFit: Aerosol containers release their contents as a fine mist of tiny droplets.

clue.text: Do trust Ted and a chum to come up to expectations

indicators.note: to do something over is to rework it, so the following words are arranged anew

explanation.surface: Trust your friends Ted and a pal to live up to what is expected of them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do' signals the rearrangement of TRUST, TED and A CHUM; 'and' and 'to' are link words. 'Do' reads like an emphatic imperative.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut the mustard is an idiom for being good enough, meeting the required standard.

clue.text: Competitors in spectacles seen around Jersey

indicators.note: seen around says the spectacles enclose the jersey

parts.note: shows are spectacles, public displays
a jersey is a knitted pullover, a jumper in British English

explanation.surface: People wearing glasses are spotted on the Channel island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spectacles' suggests glasses and 'Jersey' the Channel Island; they are SHOWS and a JUMPER (the British word for a pullover).
explanation.definitionFit: Show jumpers are riders who compete over fences in equestrian events.

clue.text: Doctor on one side looks down on leg — there is a point to it

definitions.text: there is a point to it

indicators.note: in a down answer, on means placed above what follows
looks down on means sits higher in the column, before the leg

parts.note: one is A, the indefinite article
a wing is a side, as of a building or a stage
pin is slang for a leg

explanation.surface: A doctor at the side of the bed examines a patient's leg, and there is a purpose to it.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' and 'looks down on' both mean 'placed above'. A drawing pin is the British name for a thumbtack.
explanation.definitionFit: A drawing pin, the British name for a thumbtack, has a sharp spike for fixing paper to a board.

clue.text: Most daring veteran in prime

indicators.note: in says the veteran sits within the prime

parts.note: the prime of something is its best
a veteran is old

explanation.surface: The most daring old soldier is still in his prime.
explanation.definitionFit: Boldest is the superlative of bold, meaning most courageous or adventurous.

clue.text: One can be seen in tailored worsted article

indicators.note: can be seen in says the one appears inside the tailored letters
worsted means beaten or defeated, so the letters are knocked into a new order

parts.note: one is I, the Roman numeral

explanation.surface: A tailor-made suit of fine wool fabric is on display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worsted' looks like the fabric but is the past tense of 'worst', defeat; I inside TAILORED is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: An editorial is an opinion piece written by a newspaper's editor, a kind of newspaper essay.

clue.text: Sheraton hotel's head sacked if represented as this?

definitions.text: Sheraton hotel's head sacked if represented as this?

indicators.note: sacked says the letter is dismissed from the name's pool
represented means presented again in a new arrangement of the remaining letters
the head of the hotel is its first letter

explanation.surface: Would a luxury hotel rate just this low if its manager were fired?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sacked' removes H (the head of 'hotel') from SHERATON, leaving SERATON, and 'represented' rearranges it. The whole clue also defines: a sacked boss could drop the hotel's rating.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-star rating marks the most basic grade of hotel, a poor showing for a luxury chain.

clue.text: Girl has bum of sizeable proportions

indicators.note: bum as an adjective means faulty or bad, so the letters are in poor order

explanation.surface: A rude remark about a young woman's big behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bum' looks like a noun (bottom) but is the adjective 'bad', telling you to rearrange GIRL and HAS.
explanation.definitionFit: Largish means fairly big, of moderately sizeable dimensions.

clue.text: Scruffy women tease a great deal

parts.note: to rag is to tease, in British usage
bags means lots, as in bags of time

explanation.surface: Unkempt ladies poke fun at someone a lot.
explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces are informal British: RAG means tease and BAGS means plenty.
explanation.definitionFit: A ragbag is British slang for a scruffily dressed person.

clue.text: Fair number put on short week a moment ago

parts.note: fair means just, even-handed
W is a short form for week

explanation.surface: A reasonable figure was added to an abbreviated working week only recently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put on' joins the pieces in order; 'short week' is the abbreviation W.
explanation.definitionFit: Just now means very recently, only a little while before.

clue.text: Like a feature of contract name — it's briefly on the bottom

indicators.note: briefly means each of the two words is cut to its first letter

parts.note: the rump is the bottom, the backside

explanation.surface: A signatory's name sits on the bottom line of an agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contract' is the bridge sense, the bid a side must make. 'It's' is a link word. 'Briefly' shortens 'on the' to O and T.
explanation.definitionFit: In bridge, a contract may be played without a trump suit, a no-trump contract.

clue.text: I'm a kind person: anagram to do is quick

indicators.note: quick here means lively, nimble, so the letters move about into a new order

explanation.surface: A kindly helper says sorting out a puzzle is easy work.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'anagram' is itself fodder: ANAGRAM TO DO IS is rearranged, with 'quick' as the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A Good Samaritan, from the biblical parable, is someone who helps strangers in need out of kindness.

clue.text: Crude projecting frill, so to speak

indicators.note: so to speak means the word is to be heard rather than read

parts.note: a ruff is a frilled collar that sticks out around the neck

explanation.surface: A crude Elizabethan collar, as it were.
explanation.walkthrough: A ruff is the stiff pleated collar seen in Elizabethan portraits.
explanation.definitionFit: Rough means unrefined or crude, roughly made.

clue.text: Partner for life in branch

definitions.meaning: the word paired with life in the stock phrase about risking bodily harm
a large bough of a tree

explanation.walkthrough: 'Partner for life' sounds like a spouse, but it is the word that follows 'life and' in the stock phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase life and limb pairs these words, and a limb is also a large bough of a tree.

clue.text: Showing no feeling, prisoner grabs one twice

indicators.note: grabs means the prisoner holds something inside

parts.note: an inmate is a prisoner
one can be the article AN
one is also I, the Roman numeral

explanation.surface: A convict seizes a single item and then another, without emotion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twice' asks for two different words that can each mean 'one', the article and the Roman numeral, rather than the same word repeated.
explanation.definitionFit: Inanimate means lifeless or showing no sign of life or spirit.

clue.text: Mamma's partner turning up in the end

indicators.note: turning up means the word is read upwards, in reverse, in a down answer

parts.note: Mia follows Mamma in the ABBA song title Mamma Mia

explanation.surface: Mum's partner finally appears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mamma's partner' sounds like Dad, but it is the word partnering 'Mamma' in the ABBA hit 'Mamma Mia'; 'in the' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: An aim is a goal, the purpose one works towards.

clue.text: Appropriate university prudence has backed

indicators.note: backed means the name and its possessive are read in reverse

parts.note: Pru is the usual short form of the name Prudence
has can be shortened to 's, as in she's got

explanation.surface: A university's sensible policy has supported a fitting move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prudence' looks like caution but is the woman's name, PRU; with 'has' as 'S, PRU'S turned back gives SURP.
explanation.definitionFit: To appropriate something is to take it without right, to seize it.

clue.text: Herb is a comic character

definitions.meaning: a fragrant leaf used in Italian cooking, such as pesto
a figure from comedy, such as the sitcom hotelier Fawlty

explanation.walkthrough: Basil Fawlty is the hotelier in the British sitcom Fawlty Towers; Basil Brush is a puppet fox from British children's television.
explanation.definitionFit: Basil is an aromatic cooking plant, and Basil Fawlty of Fawlty Towers and Basil Brush are famous comic figures.

clue.text: Badly designed, one's lacking in seamanship on the rocks

indicators.note: lacking in says the one is missing from the seamanship pool
on the rocks suggests a wrecked ship, so the remaining letters are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: one can be A, the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A badly built ship ran aground because its crew had poor sailing skills.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove A ('one') from SEAMANSHIP to leave SEMANSHIP, then rearrange, as 'on the rocks' signals.
explanation.definitionFit: Misshapen means deformed or wrongly formed, out of its proper shape.
